name: Databases
author: Smart Terminal
summary: Your PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite databases: browse them, edit rows, run SQL, and see what the server is doing.
description: A database tool in a tab, in the manner of pgAdmin. Save a connection to PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB, or point it at a SQLite file — paste a URL and the form fills itself in — and the tree on the left is what is there: databases, schemas, tables, views, materialized views, sequences and routines, each read from the server's own catalog. Partitions are listed apart from the tables somebody made by hand, and under More are the pages for everything else a database holds — indexes, triggers, rules, row-level security, partitioning, types, extensions, foreign data, publications and subscriptions, event triggers, languages and casts — each one what the server says, with a row that names a table leading to that table. A table opens as a grid of its rows, a page at a time, filtered by a WHERE you type and sorted by the column you click; when the table has a primary key the grid can be edited — change a cell, add a row, mark rows for deletion — and nothing is sent until you press Save, which sends all of it in one transaction or none of it. Beside the rows is the table's structure — columns, indexes, constraints, the foreign keys that leave it and the ones that arrive — and the statement that would create it. The query tool is an editor with colour, completion from the tables and columns of the database you are in, and a connection of its own per tab, so a BEGIN in one tab is that tab's transaction. Format lays a query out a clause to a line — moving whitespace and capitalising keywords, and changing nothing else — and a script can be opened from a .sql file and saved back to one. Run everything or only what is selected; each statement's answer is its own grid, an error names its line, and a query that is taking too long can be stopped. Results stop at a number of rows you choose, on the server, so SELECT * from a table of forty million rows costs what a page costs — and Export writes the whole answer to CSV, JSON or INSERT statements. The server has a page too: a dashboard of sessions, transactions, rows and blocks per second; who is connected and what each session is running, with a way to cancel a query or end a session; who is waiting on whose lock; roles, tablespaces, replication, prepared transactions and the whole configuration. A table says more than its rows: its statistics as the server counts them and as the planner believes them, which indexes are never used, what depends on it, and who may touch it. And when something is slow there is a page that asks the server why: the statements that cost the most time and the ones that are slow every time, what has been running too long, tables scanned whole for want of an index, foreign keys with no index behind them, indexes nothing uses and indexes that repeat another, tables carrying dead rows or never analysed — each with a line saying what the answer is good for, and none of it changing anything. Explain draws the plan as a tree — where the time went, node by node — and flags an estimate that was wrong by ten times or a scan that read a hundred thousand rows to keep a few. Any object can be found by a part of its name; a table or a database can be vacuumed, analysed or reindexed from its menu; and a database is backed up and restored with its own tools, pg_dump and mysqldump, to a file you choose. A table is made and changed from a form as well as from SQL: name the columns, give each a type, a default and whether it may be empty, and the statement that will be sent is on screen the whole time — written the way the engine wants it, one transaction where the engine can undo table changes and one statement where it cannot. Roles and users are made, changed and dropped from a form, and the statement shown never contains the password — it is written by the app, sent to the server, and kept nowhere. Privileges are granted and revoked for many objects and many roles at once: tick what, tick who, tick which, and read the statements before they go. A schema can be drawn: its tables as boxes with their keys marked and its foreign keys as lines, set out left to right by what refers to what, rearranged by dragging, and read by clicking a table to light up everything it touches. Two schemas can be compared — on the same server or on two — and what comes back is every table, view, sequence and routine that is only in one, or differs, with what differs said in words and the script that would make the first like the second: read first, opened in a query tab, never run by itself, and dropping nothing unless that was asked for. Rows come in from a CSV file as well as going out: the file's columns are matched to the table's by name, you see the first rows before anything happens, and the import is one transaction — a row the table refuses leaves the table as it was. And the database's own client — psql, mysql, sqlite3 — opens in a real terminal under the panel, already connected, with the password in a file only you can read rather than on the command line. A database that only another machine can reach is reached through that machine: name the SSH host and the connection, its terminal and its backups all go through a tunnel made by your own ssh, with your keys and your known hosts, so what works in a terminal works here and the app never holds a key. A setting of the server opens from the configuration page with what it accepts and when a change is felt, and is changed or put back by a statement you read first. A connection can be marked read-only, in which case nothing but a read is ever sent, or production, in which case anything that changes it stops and asks first. Everywhere, a DROP, a TRUNCATE and a DELETE or UPDATE with no WHERE stop and ask, naming the connection. Ask Claude opens a session that has been handed a table's definition, or the statement that just failed and what the server said about it. Passwords are kept by the app, encrypted; this panel never holds one and cannot reach the network at all.
